About this world

The world. A 40 × 40 torus with eight food patches that keep moving. Every food plant has an odor, an 8-bit chemical code. Whether food is nutritious or toxic follows a hidden rule over that code, and the rule changes every 3,000 ticks (pairs of bits, a staircase, triples, a single bit). Odor codes are redrawn every 100 ticks, so flies must learn the rule, not memorize odors. Flies breed when they have enough energy, and die when they starve or grow old.

The flies. Each fly has a taste learner (a set of feature masks over the odor code) and a movement learner (a set of senses). Both learn during life. A self-improving fly can also add features its own evidence supports and drop ones that stopped paying, and it watches whether its taste model actually predicts better than guessing. Children inherit the program and the evidence behind it, never the learned values.

What has been tested. In pre-registered tests on fresh worlds, self-improving flies out-competed fixed flies, a random-rewrite sham, and mutation-only evolution, and re-learned after every rule change. A separate benefit of self-improving movement on top of taste was not shown. Details: goal ladder and full log.

This is a small constructed world with hand-written learning rules. It shows bounded self-improvement inside one world — not open-ended intelligence, and not a model of real insects. Food colors on the map show the true value, which the flies cannot see.
